chapters.title: Chapter 1: Probability, Statistics, and Log‑Likelihood
chapters.description: Basic probability and statistical concepts required to formulate likelihood‑based models, derive gradients of log‑likelihood objectives, and reason about identifiability and equivalence classes of functions.
subtopics: Random variables, probability mass/density functions, conditional probability
Expectation, variance, and common inequalities
Log‑likelihood and maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
Binary classification likelihoods and the logistic (sigmoid) function
Binary cross‑entropy loss and relation to log‑likelihood
Properties of MLE: consistency, asymptotic normality
Identifiability and equivalence classes of parameterizations

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Optimization for Machine Learning
chapters.description: Optimization methods used to train neural networks and probabilistic models, including stochastic methods, regularization, and techniques for stabilizing training.
subtopics: Gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and mini‑batch methods
Adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSProp) and practical tuning
Backpropagation for sequence models
Regularization techniques (weight decay, dropout)
Gradient variance reduction and baselines
Importance weighting and reweighting examples
Constrained optimization and Lagrangian methods

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Sequence Modeling and Language Models
chapters.description: Formulation of language modeling tasks, autoregressive sequence models, conditional generation p(y | x), and the probabilistic interpretation of generated text.
subtopics: Autoregressive factorization of sequence probabilities
Conditional language modeling (p(y | x)) and sequence conditioning
Tokenization and vocabulary management
Per‑token vs sequence‑level likelihood
Maximum likelihood training for sequence models
Perplexity and likelihood‑based evaluation

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Transformer Architectures and Pretraining
chapters.description: The transformer architecture widely used in modern LMs, pretraining objectives, scaling considerations, and how pretraining yields broad capabilities.
subtopics: Self‑attention mechanism and multi‑head attention
Positional encodings and layer structure (encoder/decoder/decoder‑only)
Feedforward networks, layer normalization, residual connections
Pretraining objectives (causal LM, masked LM) and large‑scale datasets
Transfer via fine‑tuning and instruction tuning
Practical aspects: batching long sequences, memory and compute

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Decoding Strategies and Sampling from LMs
chapters.description: Methods to convert conditional probabilities into text: greedy decoding, sampling, temperature, top‑k and nucleus sampling, beam search, and their effects on diversity and quality.
subtopics: Greedy decoding and beam search
Temperature scaling and its effect on entropy
Top‑k and top‑p (nucleus) sampling
Deterministic vs stochastic decoding tradeoffs
Sequence‑level metrics and decoding hyperparameters
Best‑of‑N sampling as a selection strategy

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Supervised Fine‑Tuning and Instruction Tuning
chapters.description: Fine‑tuning pretrained LMs on task‑specific or instruction data (SFT), including practical pipelines and evaluation of fine‑tuned models.
subtopics: Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) objectives and data collection
Instruction tuning: datasets, formats, and generalization
Initialization strategies and continual fine‑tuning
Evaluation: generalization to unseen instructions
Pitfalls: overfitting to format, distribution shift

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Fundamentals of Reinforcement Learning
chapters.description: Core RL concepts needed to understand reward maximization objectives for policies, including policy/value definitions and policy gradient methods.
subtopics: Markov decision processes (states, actions, rewards, policies)
Return, discounted reward, and episodic vs continuing tasks
Policy parameterization and stochastic policies
Policy gradient theorem and REINFORCE
Baseline subtraction and advantage estimators
Entropy regularization and KL penalties in RL objectives

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Policy Optimization Algorithms and Actor‑Critic Methods
chapters.description: Practical policy optimization algorithms (PPO, TRPO, actor‑critic), their derivations, and sources of instability during training.
subtopics: Trust region methods and constrained policy updates (TRPO)
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): clipping and surrogate objectives
Actor‑critic architectures, value function learning, and bootstrapping
Variance and bias tradeoffs, value baselines
Stability issues: reward scaling, normalization, and bootstrapping failures
Practical hyperparameters and implementation considerations

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
chapters.description: The RLHF pipeline: collecting preference data, reward modeling, and optimizing a policy to match human preferences using RL, plus common practical choices.
subtopics: Collecting pairwise preference data and human annotation protocols
Reward modeling from preferences: architectures and objectives
The standard RLHF three‑stage pipeline: SFT → reward model → RL fine‑tuning
Reward normalization, baselines and partition function considerations
Common RLHF algorithms (REINFORCE, PPO) and empirical practices
Challenges: sample efficiency, instability, and distribution mismatch

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Preference and Ranking Models (Bradley‑Terry & Plackett‑Luce)
chapters.description: Statistical models for pairwise and listwise preferences, their likelihoods, identifiability issues, and how pairwise differences eliminate additive constants.
subtopics: Bradley‑Terry model for pairwise comparisons: formulation and likelihood
Plackett‑Luce model for rankings and listwise probabilities
Relation between score functions and choice probabilities (softmax over scores)
Identifiability: additive shifts and normalization constraints
MLE for preference models and gradient expressions
Extensions and practical regularization

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Control as Inference and Soft Optimal Policies
chapters.description: Interpretation of KL‑regularized control objectives as probabilistic inference, derivation of soft (Gibbs) optimal policies, partition functions, and their properties.
subtopics: KL‑regularized RL objectives and the constrained reward maximization viewpoint
Derivation of Gibbs/softmax policy π(y) ∝ π_ref(y) exp(r(y)/β)
Partition function (normalizer) properties and computational challenges
Soft value functions and their role in actor‑critic learning
Change‑of‑variables between rewards and policies under soft optimality
Practical implications: reward shaping vs policy reparameterization

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Preference‑based and Dueling Bandits
chapters.description: Bandit formulations where feedback is pairwise preferences (dueling/relative feedback), optimality notions (von Neumann winner), and offline preference learning.
subtopics: Multi‑armed bandits vs dueling bandits: problem setup
Contextual dueling bandits and contextual preference learning
Von Neumann winner and maximin strategies
Offline vs online preference data and sample complexity considerations
Algorithms for dueling bandits and regret bounds

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Statistical Learning Theory for Policies and Offline Evaluation
chapters.description: Generalization and estimation issues when learning policies from finite offline data, off‑policy evaluation, distribution shift, and consistency of estimators.
subtopics: Generalization error for policy learning and complexity measures
Off‑policy evaluation and importance sampling
Distribution shift between training (e.g., SFT samples) and deployment
Consistency of preference‑based estimators
Bias/variance tradeoffs in offline policy optimization

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Losses and Alternatives for Training Language Models from Preferences
chapters.description: Alternative objectives for aligning language models to preferences: supervised preference fine‑tuning, unlikelihood losses, and best‑of‑N approaches, with advantages and limitations.
subtopics: Supervised fine‑tuning on preferred completions (behavior cloning)
Unlikelihood training: penalizing undesired tokens or sequences
Pairwise cross‑entropy losses for preferences
Best‑of‑N selection and test‑time selection strategies
Practical tradeoffs: compute, sample efficiency, stability

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Evaluation of Generated Text and Human Judgments
chapters.description: Methods to evaluate generated text, including automated metrics, human evaluation protocols, using LMs as evaluators, and measures of correlation and reliability.
subtopics: Automatic metrics: ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR — strengths and weaknesses
Human evaluation design: pairwise comparison, Likert scales, inter‑annotator agreement
Using LMs (e.g., GPT‑4) as automated evaluators: prompting and calibration
Win‑rate metrics and tournament style comparisons
Statistical significance, sampling variance, and experiment design
Practical considerations for crowdsourcing and expert annotation

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Practical Engineering for Fine‑Tuning Large Language Models
chapters.description: Operational and implementation details that matter when fine‑tuning large LMs and training with preference data: batching, sampling during training, compute tradeoffs, and reproducibility.
subtopics: Dataset construction, prompt formatting, and pairing completions
Batching strategies for sequence data and mixed‑length sequences
Sampling from model during training vs offline datasets
Sequence‑level KL computation and tracking
Hyperparameter selection, reproducibility, and logging
Compute and memory considerations; distributed training patterns
